At such a moment as this, what is it? *He strikes the meditation desk once.* He says: "A gust of west wind comes; two or three leaves fall."
Small Assembly Sermon for the Retreat: Severing the master’s seat, do not fall into a secondary view. A single thought is ten thousand years; ten thousand years are a single thought.
If you proceed in this manner, these one hundred and twenty days of summer retreat are not yet the long term.
If this is not yet so, Mount Mao has another expedient: when exhausted, there is change; with change, there is penetration. When the cup is dashed to the ground, the plate becomes a bowl.
Seven or eight pieces. [The Master] strikes the meditation staff once.

The Small Sermon for the End of the Summer Retreat: The summer retreat of one hundred and twenty days has now concluded. Regarding the single phrase within it, take care not to transmit it erroneously.
Is there anyone among you who has attained thorough mastery? If so, come forward and, taking error as error, utter a single word.
Look! If you can speak of it, the donkey in the back garden eats grass; if you cannot speak of it, the wild geese carry reeds as autumn arrives.

This is the small *prātimokṣa* assembly for the winter night: when the six lines of the hexagram are exhausted, the demons of darkness naturally perish; when the single Yang line returns, my Way prospers greatly.
Dongshan’s “sweetmeats” were an extraordinary arrangement; Old Hao’s cotton trousers remained as bright red as before. At Mount Mao, the few cannot withstand the many.
Meeting one another, we follow custom and say, “It is a severe cold in the middle winter. We simply wish that everyone will take care of themselves in accordance with the season.
But if we count from the beginning, there is clearly a great matter at hand. Why? Because nine times nine is eighty-one.
First: Only after the pauper has finished suffering his retribution does he finally stretch out his legs to sleep. Mosquitoes, gadflies, and fleas rush out to rescue him—how urgent!

This is the small *cán* (private instruction) for the summer retreat. When the wind is calm and the waves are still, one must strictly avoid letting one's heels droop. Under the bright sun and clear sky, one ought to withdraw.
Mount Mao opens a single thread of the Way; let us deliberate upon it together for a moment.
Suddenly, he ties up the mouth of his cloth bag, until even the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are transformed back into mountains, rivers, and the great earth.

Having swallowed up the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, where, after all, can you monks vent your breath? *He slaps the meditation seat and says:* "No one knows this meaning. *He gives the command.*

I recall Nanquan’s small *saman* after the summer retreat: a single thought at the gateway of the face, uninterrupted for a long duration, seeing the perfected sentence, complete in its hundred flavors.

If we discuss "binding," one should remain settled in their own place; it is not a matter of dragging things short to make them long. As for "untying," one proceeds spontaneously according to circumstances;
it is likewise not a matter of dragging things long to make them short. Yellow gall is sweet and licorice is bitter; cast upon the ground, gold rings with a metallic sound like mere filth.
Muzhou forced Yunmen’s leg to break; Nanquan did not beat the drum of Yanguan. (He strikes his staff once.)
Winter Night Small Sermon: The Buddhas did not appear in this world; the Patriarchs did not come from the West. This blunt and straightforward phrase—Nanyue facing up to Tiantai.
A person of keen intelligence does not dwell in deliberation; for those of impatient nature, what need is there to raise it again?
Just sit as you are, and you will sink into the mud on level ground. If you intend to step forward further, a creeping vine-snake will coil around your feet. Have you not seen at Yuquan?
Old Master Hao said: "The movement of the sun's shadow shifts; though my trousers are bright red, it is not that they have not been washed, for there has been nothing to replace them.
After a long silence, he said: "In the midst of the strife of war throughout ancient and modern times, how many have reached this state of peace?"
A Small Sermon on New Year’s Eve: The old year departs this very night; yet as it departs, it truly does not depart. The new year arrives tomorrow;
yet as it arrives, it truly does not arrive. Ten thousand ages of the vast sky remain unchanged, while the revolving sun and moon merely hasten in their empty course.
I, this mountain monk, report it thus: perhaps someone among you who cannot bear it will come forward and say, "This is just the talk of the Great and Small Yung-wang!"
"Two stakes. And how about this? I simply send them away. Even so, it must be genuine before it will do.
Nowadays, many monks have similar speech, yet their local jurisdictions differ; thus, to err by a hair’s breadth is to lose by a thousand miles.
He struck his staff once and said, "Who recognizes that Yama is a ghost?"

Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat: If one were to uphold the true command and grasp the essential principles, it would require that on the road of the Precious Banner, wild grass reaches to the heavens, and before the Peak of the Jade Desk, thorns and brambles fill the ground—even this would not yet be considered extraordinary.

How much more so when three hundred or five hundred people gather their heads together, whispering and engaging in vast deliberations; how truly a shame! Tonight, at Yuyang, having no other choice, I shall briefly [speak].
Borrowing the path of the ancients' expedient means, I shall accompany you all to reach the appointed destination. After a long silence, he said:

"Taking Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery, I dwell in peace within body and mind through the Wisdom of Equality. It is neither 'not' nor 'is'; it is neither 'is' nor 'is not. A tiger bites a tiger;
a snake swallows its own snout. Nevertheless, you must not move a muscle. If you move, I shall break your legs."

Donkey-waisted. On this New Year’s Eve small *chan* session, there is no place to enter; it is utterly already accomplished. At the very moment of perfect correspondence, there is not a shred of a handle.
On Vulture Peak, Kāśyapa’s transmission was false; at Shaolin, the entrustment to Shen Guang was in vain. As for all other lineages and the branching of the lamps, they cannot avoid—
They humiliate one another. Even now, on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, does each of you not know it is the eve of the New Year?
Yet you still come here, clutching your staffs against your chests, listening intently for what?
I, this mountain monk, have never distinguished between good and evil; to further seize, drag, and tear apart people before you is utterly groundless. Why is that? Because...
This renunciant, regarding the lifting of the retreat, offers this small discourse: I take Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery; body and mind dwell in peace within the wisdom of equanimity.
This is what is meant by "binding" from the fifteenth day of the fourth month, and likewise "lifting" on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
It was thus before the time of King Vimalacitra; it will be thus when Maitreya Buddha descends to birth.
Ten thousand years are a single thought-moment; a single thought-moment is ten thousand years. There is no past and no present; there is no change and no difference.
To go on like this is to sit squarely within the nest of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, unable to emerge. Some fellows then say: "What does the community of patch-robed monks have to do with this?"
It is certainly so. If you insist on acting as you please and sitting as you please— defecating in your alms bowl, spitting into your water jar,

disparaging the Buddha, slandering the Dharma, refusing to count among the assembly, and cultivating the causes of the ten unwholesome paths until you accomplish the five crimes of immediate retribution—
if you proceed in this manner, you will once again fall into the trap of the present moment, having no means of transcending it.
The Path. Even if you were to cut off both "it being so" and "it not being so" all at once, and have another way of life, even upon examination, it would still not suffice.
Why? Because you have again fallen into your own old nest and cannot turn yourself around.
Now, it is easy to escape the nest of Vulture Peak, but it is difficult to escape the nest of the present day. To escape the nest of the present...
At that time, it is easy to remain within the old nest; however, to emerge from one’s own nest is difficult.

Since this is so, how can one get out? [The Master] takes up his staff, strikes once, and says: "The nest of Vulture Peak, the nest of the present age, and one's own nest—struck once, they are all pulverized. At this point, what should be done? He looks to his left and right and says:
"Last night, where did this fire come from? It has burned out the ancient tombs.

A small *sǎn* (private instruction) for the summer retreat: On the road to Caoxi, waves rise pointlessly into mounds; Before Mount Yujing, who would believe the ground is as level as the palm of a hand?
Coming and going are without interval; movement and stillness share a single source. Stretching forth a hand, one touches upon the Great Dharma of Bodhidharma.
The Master’s eyes: he raises his foot and steps forward, trampling through the nostrils of Old Śākyamuni. There is no evasion; all contrivance is utterly severed.
What more need be said of long or short periods? It is simply a matter of one’s own heart being willing and one’s mind being resolved.
Since this is so, how exactly should one practice throughout these ninety days? Let the root of the staff take hold and cease.
Use scissors. Since the alms bowl has no handle, there is no need to attach one.

Small Sermon upon the Resolution of the Summer Retreat: When the faculty does not leave its station, one sinks into the land of intoxication; when speech does not leave its nest, one is stuck in the golden net.
He held up his staff and said, "Look! Look! Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja is now upon the tip of this mountain monk’s staff, performing for all of you the ritual of *pravāraṇā*.
He extensively expounds the Dharma-gates attained and realized within the ninety days of this summer retreat, as well as the practices and vows cultivated;
these are fully present in every person, identical in each and every case, reaching directly to the West."
When all the disciples of the Buddha at Nālandā Monastery heard this, there was not one who did not join their palms in praise, exclaiming that it was wonderful and unprecedented.

Only you lot, a pack of fellows, are like those who try to hold back water with a stone; remaining unperturbed as if nothing were happening, and finding yourselves at a loss for what to do, you have retreated into Mount Mārīcī.
A Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat: The ten directions gather together as one—how so? Each and every one studies non-action; what leisure is there for such toil?
This is the field where Buddhas are chosen, yet it deceives and kills people. When the mind is empty, one returns with the highest degree; for now, stay outside the triple gate.
I, this mountain monk, have thus announced it. But tell me, where does the crux lie? Do you all know?
The fundamental nature is the same for all under heaven.

At the small *cān* (private instruction) upon the conclusion of the summer retreat, he held up his staff and addressed the assembly, saying: "To realize it alone and transcendently is still not free from confusion. He struck the ground with the staff.
It is as before; yet there still remains that which looks back and reflects. One must indeed tear open the mouth of the cloth bag and thrust out the tip of the staff.

When gain and loss are both forgotten and right and wrong are entirely extinguished, the wisdom of all wisdoms is pure—without duality, without division, without distinction, and without interruption.
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra raise their staffs and say: "In this very place, perform the ritual of self-indulgence."
Now tell me, where is Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva? (He strikes the meditation desk once. He says: "Do not recognize the 'not-hearing' at the moment of hearing.

Having gone out on patrol and arrived at the Dharma hall, after the head monk has finished holding the whisk during the winter night, he requests a small *paramārtha* (small *cán*). If you can understand it in this very way, then you have truly attained it.
It is already late—second watch, third watch. Should you hesitate, I cannot help but rely on the majestic light of the host to attend this occasion.
(Holding up the staff) This is a settled case, not involving any contrivance. Vertical or horizontal, all comes from here.
Heaven and earth rely on it for their covering and bearing; the sun and moon rely on it for their circulation; the four seasons rely on it for their succession.
"Thank you. By this, all things flourish and bloom. *He strikes the board once.* He says, "The myriad yin energies have been stripped away; the multitudes of demons have already been exterminated.
*He strikes the board once more.* He says, "The single yang energy returns; my Way prospers greatly. At that moment, Venerable Fuhu could not restrain himself;
he gave the back of National Teacher Guoyi a slap and laughed heartily, saying, "How shameful! How shameful! Wind.
The rains fall in their proper season; the *sū* and *hú* rice ripen, and the world is sufficient. Both the eastern neighbor and the western neighbor are all patrons of Master Wánglǎo.
Tell me, how does one teach and transform them at this point? He strikes the meditation desk once and says: "One must be the Abbot, the Senior Teacher, to do so."
A Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat: A single push and it turns; yet this still involves traversing a path. Three times knocking and not returning—thus it is difficult to maintain a fixed position.
Have you not seen the butcher Guang'e lay down his cleaver and say, "I am counted among the thousand Buddhas"?
Or the Mara Zangbi who said, "Wait until all sentient beings have attained Buddhahood, until the realm of sentient beings is emptied, and even until there are no longer any sentient beings..."
"Only after the names were given was I able to give rise to the Bodhicitta.

Even if you were to drive a stake through your brains and dip them in glue, you lot still gather here in a circle, lighting fires together, saying, 'We observe the *jinzu* retreat and dwell in seclusion to realize enlightenment within a fixed period.
But what exactly do you intend to realize? Is there any blood beneath your skin? [The Master] struck the meditation seat with his whisk once.
[The Master] said: "When it is time to return at nightfall, return; do not wait for the break of dawn and lose the rooster.
Winter Night Small Sermon: Cutting off head-on, the frozen lock seals the cold pond; Holding it forth face-to-face, warmth returns to the secluded valley.
He raised his whisk and said, "Look, look! The Spirit-Response Dragon King and National Teacher Guoyi congratulate one another.
How joyful that the first yang has returned; our Way shall flourish greatly. Once again, the halls and pavilions within Mount Shuangjing are seen renewed."
The prices of rice and salt at the crossroads remain as they were before; let us set this aside for a moment. But consider this:
when the practitioner Jue-zhi gave a single shout to a flat stone, it was split into seven pieces and eight fragments. Was this, then, the marvelous function of spiritual power?

"Is this, moreover, simply the nature of things (*dharmatā*) being thus? After a long silence, he said: 'The Big Dipper turns east; the Southern Dipper shifts west. This is the Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat:
Outside the mind there is no dharma; outside dharmas there is no mind. When speech issues forth, it is not sound; before form appears, it is not an object."
The moment you open your mouth, you touch upon the ancestral taboo name of the Sovereign of Emptiness; the moment you intend to take a step, you tread upon the heels of Maitreya.
Every single thing is one’s own livelihood; every place is nothing other than wondrous function. Therefore it is said:
"Taking great perfect enlightenment as my monastery, body and mind dwell in peace within the wisdom of equanimity. *Psh!* Under the gate of Caoxi, one must strictly avoid worldly talk.

A Small *Chanshan* (Private Assembly) for the End of the Summer Retreat: To employ the mind to employ the mind only increases one's transgressions; to use wisdom to dispel wisdom only reveals that the illness is deepening. Thus it is said:
"If a household lacks the *Bai-ze* (White Deer) diagram, such demonic apparitions will surely not occur;

if the kitchen lacks scraps of food to gather flies, hunger and emptiness will naturally be forever severed. This mountain monk has been coming and going throughout this summer retreat, yet I have not uttered a single word.
People assist and benefit one another; yet they still crave a single pot of soup. But tell me, can there be mouse droppings placed within it?
After a long silence, he said: "Ugh! Tonight, for no reason at all, two have fallen."
Winter Night Small Sermon Two winters have passed within this earthen and wooden place. In the morning there is haste, and in the evening there is haste.

From the beginning, the karmic consciousness has had no basis to rely upon; what need is there to speak of Dongshan’s great "empty talk"? It has reached the point where there is no Chan to be studied and no Way to be learned.
Where shall the Chan practitioners of the four seas find a place to settle? Gazing toward the eastern ocean from the Hanhui Pavilion, [one looks up at] Mount Lingxiao.
I bow my head to Nanyue; I laugh at Old Longya. In his hand he holds a broken wooden ladle. On this New Year’s Eve small *chan* assembly:
when Gautama appeared in the world, he played with the false as if it were real; when Bodhidharma came from the West, there was much emptiness and little substance.
As for the rest, they manifest great capacity and display great function; they dally with spiritual transformations and race with the sharp edge of their rhetoric.
Yet when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, it is still nothing more than the eve of the New Year. When Jing-shan makes such an announcement, does it have no merit?
(He strikes the meditation seat with his whisk and says: "What can it possibly be worth?"
A Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat: In a state of helplessness, a dog licks the oil cauldron; when all skillful means are exhausted, a cat sees grain.
One must simply ensure that the eyes do not hang upon the door and the mind does not dwell on the profound. A step taken loses its trace; a word turned stirs up offense.

One knows not the difference between the long and short months—what need is there to speak of long-term or short-term retreats? Worldly affairs are in turmoil and days and months are busy; the single body is but a blur.
The vastness of heaven and earth is narrow. At such a time as this, tell me: is there still a way to emerge? After a long silence, he said:
"Whether with merit or without merit, do not let your belly go empty."
Small *Chanshi* for the end of the summer retreat: Words cannot unfold the matter; speech does not meet the occasion. Those who rely on words perish; those who linger in phrases are deluded.
Seven Southern Dippers, eight Northern Dippers. At Lu Shan’s Arhat Temple, three novices are ordained each year;
at Jing Shan Monastery, there are two gruels and one meal every day. Within these ninety days, you all hold your alms bowls and face toward—
On the long bedstead, they eat and drink to their heart's content. Among them, is there anyone who knows what it means to be full? Their entire bodies are rice;
their entire bodies are water. When questioned, these dull-witted ones know nothing at all.

A small-scale *sancha* (general address) for the end of the summer retreat. A monk asked, "When the Field for Selecting Buddhas opens and the atmosphere of the monastic groves is renewed, who is it that attains the 'Pass' with an empty mind?
The Master said, "There is only you, and you are not [it]. The monk pressed further, "What about Chan Master Fojian?
The Master said, "I am not it either. The monk said, "In that case, everyone everywhere enjoys peace and prosperity."
The Master said, "I, this old monk, am not like you, Senior. The student stepped forward and asked, "In the past, while Guishan was seated, Yangshan and Xiangyan were standing in attendance.
Guishan said, 'Nowadays, those who act thus are few; those who do not act thus are many. At such a time, what would it be like?
The Master said, "There is bait on the hook. The student asked, "When Yangshan moved from east to west, what then? The Master—
[The Master] said, "A single cast and it comes up. The student asked, "When Xiangyan went from west to east, what was that? The Master said, "There is no different soil in the same pit.
The student asked, "When Yangshan and Xiangyan responded in such a manner, did they accord with the intention of Master Muzhou? The Master said, "..."
[The Master] said, "I suspect there is no connection. The student asked, "Tangshan said, 'This matter, thirty years from now, will be cast to the ground and make a golden sound.
What about that? The Master said, "Not fit to feed a dog. The student asked, "Yangshan said, 'This must be promoted by the Master himself before it can be so.
The Master said, "That was not a kind intention. The student asked, "Xiangyan said..."
[The student] said, "Even now, there are not few. The Master said, "The entire family line has been lost. [The student] stepped forward and asked, "Miaoyan said, 'Shut that dog's mouth!
Did he approve of him or not? The Master said, "Water chestnuts from Suzhou; lotus roots from Shaobo. [The student] asked, "Miaoyan gave such an instruction;
today, with the great assembly standing before you, what instruction do you, Jingshan, have? The Master said, "Hunger."
When hungry, he eats; when weary, he sleeps. When the monk prostrated, he said: "Open the mouth of the cloth bag; smash through the iron gate-bar.
Whether ordinary or holy, one may go north or south without hindrance. To the left or to the right, naturally there are openings through seven holes and eight apertures.
When speaking reaches where action cannot reach, and when acting reaches where speech cannot reach, the 'blow-off blade' is held in hand—how chilling!"

The majestic divine power is chilling. A precious mirror faces the window; its radiance is limpid and clear. How could the myriad dharmas ever disturb it? Even the thousand sages do not share its precincts.
It settles all within the world while uniquely manifesting beyond all forms. At such a time, let us not speak of Mañjuśrī spending the summer retreat in three places;
but why was he unable to emerge from the woman’s samādhi when at the gathering place of all Buddhas? There is much more to this small matter.
The government offices are closed; in the empty mountains there are spirits and ghosts.

During the summer retreat, I give a small *śamaya* discourse. As I gather medicines and store them for the sick, those who recover grow more numerous. Yet as I break the measures and snap the scales, the disputes become even more intense.
"It is not so," you cannot say. "It is not not so," you cannot say. "Both so and not so," you cannot say.
Only then can Jingshan and all of you, in a place where there is no connection, together partake of this and dwell in this—forgetting that and forgetting this, neither real nor unreal.
At the two meals, the strength from the gruel and rice is coarse; let me ask you all: do you understand?
None. A Small Evening Sermon on the Eve: The old year is the new year; the new year is the old year. To know the year that is new, one must realize it is fundamentally the year that is old.
At this point, to add a single grain of weight makes the scale’s tail soar upward; to subtract a single hair makes the measuring rod fall short.
The head is short; one must let go from the void. Where it falls, there is peace; naturally, the vital energy (*qi*) flows through in hidden harmony.
Warmth arises in the secluded valley, and the myriad things display an air of flourishing growth. The primal pivot forgets its work of nurturing;

the moon in the water is mindless, and wind and clouds differ of their own accord. At such a time as this, what is it? "Not picking up dropped items on the road" is the true ancient way; all the people...
Delighting in karma, one beholds a bountiful year.

This small summer retreat *śamatha-vipaśyanā* discourse transcends conceptual thought and linguistic expression; its principle is beyond the categories of correct and biased. The pestle pounds toward the southeast; the millstone grinds toward the northwest.

The浑仑 (húnlún) is without seams or fissures; it is level and plain, free from contradiction or error. The Buddhas of the three periods, whether speaking horizontally or vertically, merely display their verbal prowess.
The Patriarchs of successive generations, whether raising the teaching fully or partially, vainly produce knots and complications.
Within these ninety days and throughout the twelve hours of the day, how shall you all enter? How shall you tread? How shall you make use of it? [He] raises his whisk.
The Master said: "If you can understand it here, I will grant that you may dissolve the ten voids within the tip of a hair and place kalpas of dust within a single thought.
At every moment you shall keep your feet restrained; in every place you shall dwell in peace. From head to foot, there shall be seven holes and eight apertures.
But if this is not yet so, then the partitioned doors inside the Buddha Hall will block and suffocate you to death."

A Small Sermon upon the Conclusion of the Summer Retreat: In Jiangnan and the two Zhe regions, spring is cold and autumn is hot; the events of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust exist in this very moment.
This present moment is no different from those kalpas of motes of dust. If you can see it thus, all of you have been constantly at home throughout these ninety days.
There was never a time when I did not go out and come in together with the mountain monk.
While the mountain monk was traveling abroad for ninety days, there was never a moment when I did not rise and fall together with all people;

I perceived not the slightest trace of "self" or "other," nor did I perceive the slightest mark of separation or union. All was suddenly vast and empty, transcendent and uniquely liberated. Although it is thus...
It is so. Now tell me: when this mountain monk calls you all from within the city of Chang’an, will you respond from atop Mount Wufeng?
If you can respond, then everything spoken above is entirely without falsehood.
If it is otherwise, it will bring such misfortune upon this mountain monk that my tongue shall be plowed for days without end.

Winter Night Small Sermon: Cold comes and heat goes, yet this small plot of ground has never wavered. When the drum falls silent and the bell ceases, the assembly on Vulture Peak remains as if it had never dispersed.
If you can understand it in this way, you will see that Sudhana did not leave his original position to enter the lands within the pores of Samantabhadra;

Having paid his respects to his acquaintance, once the business of the day was concluded, he returned before Mount Jing and stood with a deep bow.

At this time, the monasteries throughout the land perform great Buddhist rites—some selecting the 'fruit' of Dongshan, some raising the 'loincloth' of Old Hao, some citing the 'tea' of Zhaozhou, and some displaying the 'cake' of Yunmen."
How grand their deliberations! They are truly bustling and heated. Here, however, it is merely cold and silent, empty and desolate.
Hearing nothing to hear, attaining nothing to attain—what is your intention, Master? *Tu!* Have you not heard it said:
"I have heard that in ancient times, the customs were simple and crude"?
A Small Sermon on the Eve of the New Year: The passage of time is as fleeting as a rushing river. The old year has passed, and now the new year arrives.
Year after year, they come and go of their own accord; yet how could there ever be any change in this fundamental reality?

If you understand it thus, then this year is just so, next year will be just so, and the year after that, and even for hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions of years—it shall remain just so.
Just so. Just so, just so. Have you all ever seen the principle that does not undergo change?
Leaves sprout on trees in spring and return to the earth in autumn; the sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night.
A Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat. The six directions and nine realms—sentient beings and the non-sentient alike—are all here, as I hold up my whisk.
Under the decree of Mount Jing, you are not permitted to take a single step in vain, nor may you utter a single word in vain.
Speaking must reach the point where speech cannot arrive; practicing must reach the point where practice cannot arrive. How can one practice at the point where speech cannot arrive?
Only one who is footless can do so. How can one speak at the point where practice cannot arrive? Only one who is tongueless can do so.
If one can speak it, then a single phrase becomes a thousand phrases and ten thousand phrases, with every phrase returning to the source. If one can practice it...
One step, a thousand steps, ten thousand steps—step by step, one treads firmly upon reality. Now, what is the principle of treading firmly?
It is said: "A person with clear eyes falls into a well."
New Year’s Eve Small Sermon: From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past, there has been a direct transmission, branching out into various schools that now pervade heaven and earth.
If one examines this closely, it is nothing other than one person deceiving another; it is merely a matter of mutual deception.
Nevertheless, even so, one must truly be able to deceive oneself before one can succeed. If you only know how to deceive others but cannot deceive yourself, [it is of no avail].
This person has hands but no eyes; if he can deceive himself, he cannot deceive others. This person has eyes but no hands;
if he can deceive himself, he can also deceive others. I venture to guarantee that this person is fully endowed with both hands and eyes.
It is like being in the bright daylight, seeing all manner of objects; one takes and gives them as the hand moves, without any doubt or obstruction.

Naturally, one is not shifted by cold or heat, nor moved by the turning of the seasons. Furthermore, it does not hinder one from seeing people celebrating the winter solstice—celebrating the winter solstice—or seeing people celebrating the New Year—celebrating the New Year.

The Verse on the Summer Retreat (*Varṣā*): "To protect life, one must kill; only when all are killed does one enter the retreat.
If you can grasp the meaning within this, an iron boat will float upon the water. All the assembly received these instructions in silence.

Having slain them all, he then severs his own head. Because the head has been severed, there is no one capable of severing it.
When the great assembly witnessed this event, they all realized the non-arising of dharmas. Jing Mountain followed this with joy.

I briefly record the date: the eighteenth day of the eighth month of the year Kǎishí (1253) of the Shàodìng era.
On this day, the tide at Qiántáng was greater than usual, and spectators gathered like a wall. Those who went out to meet the tide were beyond counting;
their emerging and submerging, their coming and going, were like mere child’s play. Yet among them, there were some who could not emerge. Why? Has it not been said: "Playing with the tide"?
One must be a person who can ride the tide.
To the attendant Xiyen, I say:
studying the Way is like a great merchant of the world traversing the vast ocean; when it is boundlessly limitless, one must first rely upon a boat and oars, and apply diligent effort.
The oars of the watchtower. When one arrives there, it takes but a moment. At that very instant, looking back at all the effort previously exerted, it all ceases at once.
In this immediate state, one is naturally settled and secure; rare treasures and wondrous jewels all manifest before one, for these are now one's own original possessions.
Only then can one distribute wealth to the poor and relieve the needy, employing them as one pleases, without depending on anything else.

Others! Have you not seen that in the past, when Sudhana traveled through one hundred and ten cities and visited fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), each spiritual friend bestowed upon him a specific dharma-gate?
Yet, in the end, these were all limited. Later, amidst the sound of Maitreya’s finger-snap, he entered the Great Pavilion;
he suddenly forgot what he had previously realized, and original wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) manifested before him—only then can it be called the Unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*).
Only through this dharma-gate of limited measure can one be said to have attained great sovereign enjoyment.

At that time, had Sudhana not attained this single realization, he would have merely gained broad soles from his travels. Attendant Yen has come ten thousand *li* to the south to wander across rivers and lakes;
I imagine the spiritual friends you have encountered must be numerous. Yet, regarding what you have realized, you must surely surpass Sudhana.
It would be best for them to remain at the level of ordinary beings.
To show that elder disciples do not practice Chan and junior masters do not listen to the teachings— just as if they were suddenly and truly not practicing at all.
I do not listen. I step directly down upon the heels of Gautama before he was born, and I grasp the nostrils of Bodhidharma before he arrived.
I bind these two old barbarians together into a single bundle, set them upright on their heads, and let them collapse while urinating.

Is this not the mark of a truly outstanding man? Should you, however, follow the traces of mud or cling to words, you will—as before—be thrust into the bag of antiquated relics; there is no escaping it.
This marks the period of liberation. The monk Sheng of Jiading is a foremost disciple of Qingxi of Nengren.
He visited me at Mount Jing and, stepping forward, said: "Since the day I left my teacher, I have informed him that I wish to visit Zhongshan and then Mount Shuangjing.
I have already received a Dharma discourse from the Venerable Chijue; I wear his teachings upon my person and dare not slacken in the slightest. [He then] withdrew it from his sleeve...
This paper wick incense—furthermore, I wish for this old monk to lend him a hand. Therefore, I say to him:
"You deserve sixty blows of the staff for abandoning your teacher to seek elsewhere; you deserve twenty blows for having accepted the 'smearing' of Zhongshan;
you deserve twenty blows for coming to this old monk's place and still speaking at length without ceasing. Just as I was about to take up my staff...
The staff was not there; it was sent back together with [the offender] to Nengren for disciplinary action. Later, he suddenly became aware of his own pain and itching.
We three have all committed the offense of *duṣkṛta*. [Thus] it was shown to the venerable Candrottarā.
When a student first enters the Way, it is like the new moon, appearing curved and crooked. By the time it reaches the full moon, it is perfectly round;

its pure light pervades the ten directions, illuminating all that is hidden. Yet, one still remains within the realm of light and shadow, sitting beside the side of the Dharma, having not yet attained the path of total penetration.
Therefore, one must proceed from the sixteenth night onward, gradually wearing away [all traces] until—
In the darkness, it is no different from when it has not yet arisen. At such a time, it cannot be told to others, nor can it be presented to others;

it can only be known by oneself. If there is even the slightest trace of it remaining unexhausted, it becomes a leakage, and one will be ranked among those standing downwind, joining their palms behind people's backs. This does not apply to those of the highest capacity—does it not?
Seeing Guling returning from his travels, the Master asked, "During your journey through the various regions, how much Buddha-dharma have you learned?
Guling replied, "It is exactly as it was before I ever left. "Ha! [the Master exclaimed]. "To open one's mouth and immediately emit the stench of excrement!
Monk Yue had followed him for a very long time; he was earnest in his pursuit of the Way and was truly admirable. Now, however, with his teacher and father still living in the hall, he intends—
He returned home to visit his parents. Before departing, he lit incense and requested a parting word from the Master.
The Master then said to him, "When you return and meet with your teacher, if he should ask you about this or that, by all means do not act like Guling and present such a confused, muddled response."
I fear that if one were to imitate the conduct of Deshan, then both this scroll of mine and that [scroll] would be treated together as mere paper wiped for cleaning.

To say that the words shown to Abbot Ning are a deception, and his silence is a slander—beyond speech and silence, there is another aperture; from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old, it has never been thus.
If you dare to look with the eye of direct realization, although Deshan and Linji exerted their utmost strength to lift it up, they remained on the left side, merely pointing with their fingers;
they never once moved a single hair’s breadth of its true settled state.
If you wish to truly shoulder this burden, you must investigate it before even the formation of the womb. Otherwise, even if...
"Having mastered the art of holding water so that not a drop leaks, one cannot avoid leaving home and losing one's livelihood;
it is evident that this matter is extremely difficult to bear. Having written thus far, Ning came forward, bowed, and then shouted: 'Stop! Stop!
Even before I left Jiading, I already knew that the Great Buddha was sitting atop Mount Jiuding. To this very day, I have been unable to turn my body. It is you, old man, alone! "
With water dripping from his mouth, I dare say he has not yet reached the bottom. Alas! Having played with horses for thirty years, today he is knocked down by a donkey.
—Shown to Layman Shi Hou.
The ancients followed the Way; throughout all quarters, the discourse on Chan was vast and expansive. How can that compare to my here-and-now, where one tills the fields to earn a meal?
Though this may seem like a soft and easygoing approach, when viewed alongside the majesty of Guliang splitting Mount Taihua, it is still not as fierce.
Furthermore, there are those who let out a great "ha-ha" laugh upon hearing the sound of the wooden board, yet when the time comes for them to strike the gong, they claim they are hungry.
It is for this reason that one rejoices. How could this ever be a matter of letting loose the lips of a donkey or displaying the clumsy bag of a fool?
Nowadays, those who investigate the Way often fail to grasp the fundamental source; they act impulsively, spilling excrement and urine at every turn—truly laughable! O Master Hou.
A true practitioner of the robe must not conform to the crowd; only when one sees this and employs a dustpan and broom for their work can they be considered fit.
This was shown to the Administrative Monk (Jian-si) Xiang. Jian-si was the chief disciple of my elder brother, Master Shitian; he left his own teacher to follow me in study many years ago.
At first he was assigned to the Office of Attendants, and later to the Office of the Treasury. Someone remarked, "Xiangshuang is a man of exceptional talent;
he is no creature confined within a cage. They considered me mistaken. I replied, "In the past, Yangqi assisted Ciming and propagated the Way of Fenyang.
When he was pressed by Ciming during the evening assembly, this was but a minor detail. Yet when he later appeared in the world, he said, 'The Head of the Monastery (Hui) understands Chan.'"
It is not merely that they were unaware at one particular time. Regarding what Cuoyan said—that "Ciming’s Buddha-dharma was like a single boat:
first Daining, then Huanglong, and finally himself"—he did not mention Yangqi.
Was this also due to ignorance? Or is it because it cannot be easily conjectured? Furthermore, he subsequently [upheld] the orthodoxy of Linji.
As for the continuity that remains unextinguished from generation to generation, how could it be burdened by the distinction between the pure and the turbid?

What is called "not knowing" is indeed not false. You, Xiang, should know that for others not to know you is not the ultimate state; rather, it is only when you yourself do not know [your own self] that you are truly perfected.
To the Chan guest Shideng:
Shideng is a veteran general from the field of Dharma-battle. Whenever one enters the fray, one must settle the matter at hand;

one must have the seven essentials by one's side and be fully equipped with both strategy and tactics. In arranging one’s meaning and phrases according to the occasion, every move must demonstrate a way of emergence.
On this path, every step possesses the mechanism of both life and death. Sometimes one draws a bow with the back turned; sometimes one enters directly with a single blade;

sometimes one meets the vanguard and pierces the target; sometimes one feigns defeat and drags the banner. Thus, there is the act of bearing up, the borrowing of circumstances, and the practice of the mind.
There are those who are prone to stumbling; were their hands to slip or their feet to falter for but a moment, their very lives would fall into the hands of others.

Because Dēngzhēn grasped the essential point, he was able to preserve his person and stay far from harm. When facing the enemy lines on the battlefield, the veteran masters of various quarters often found themselves powerless against him;
yet before Jìngshān, he still dared to meet him with weapons raised. Thus, holding this scroll, he lowered [his head]...
Feeling abashed, he stepped forward and said, "I have long relied upon your venerable presence, yet I have never been able to apply myself to the tools of practice you have previously taught.
Now, in your presence, I request a different question. The Master replied accordingly: "Close off the throat, lips, and mouth."
Setting this aside for a moment, let me ask you something.
This junior monk, De-tong, is a guest from the Chan community.
He is one of my less worthy disciples, yet he has served me for the longest time; however, I have often been troubled by his talkative nature and have frequently wished—
I stripped him of his patched robe and gave him a severe beating. Once he had silently grasped my meaning, he departed for a tour of Mount Lu; it was clearly an escape from this situation.
Furthermore, he dared to use humble words to request a single phrase for self-reflection on the road. To be respectful yet devoid of propriety is truly intolerable.
Nevertheless, as the saying goes, "A wrathful fist does not strike a smiling face. Thus, I took up my brush and said to him: [The subsequent verse follows.]
It is time to depart; you should return early. Although I do not bathe in my old age, I wish for you to wash my feet so as not to disappoint my vow.
This was shown to the attendant Nihon (who resided at Tōfuku-ji).
The Way has no north or south; its propagation depends on the person. If one can truly propagate the Way, then every place is entirely a field of enjoyment.
Abiding in the unmoving fundamental limit, one traverses throughout the southern direction; without engaging in seeking, one universally associates with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Thus, there is not even a hair’s breadth of separation between this land and that land.

As for reaching the very end of the boundless seas of fragrant water, and beyond that, further beyond—that is as easy as pointing at one's own palm. This is the constant nature of my own mind; it does not depend on anything external.
As for other arts, if one can attain such faith and achieve such thorough insight, then crossing oceans and deserts, ascending ridges and mountains, will not be considered difficult at all.
You, my attendant, emulate Sudhana in his travels through a hundred cities to seek out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), resolving to clarify the great matter of your own person;
your resolve is no small one. Since you have offered incense and requested words, I have written this to show you.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fojian, Volume Three;
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fojian, Volume Four: General Discourses (Pushe).
"Excellent! Strike the board three times. Friends and acquaintances all come to attend; since you already know the proper timing, I shall not repeat myself.
If one relies on such a report, it is already a burying of all people.
Even if one were to realize the time for themselves before the board has even sounded, that would still not save half of them—how much less can they bear to gather in groups of threes and twos?
Ears pressed to head, hands clasped at the chest—listen here to this mountain monk’s jargon. How truly degrading! Each and every one of you is a man of great capacity;
each and every one has traveled the pilgrimage paths. Who is without their share? Why do you not rouse yourselves?
Take up your sitting cloths and strike me right on the mouth! Overthrow the meditation seat and walk away with arms flung out! Would that not be a source of joy and liberation?
Although this is so, one must actually reach such a state before it can be attained. Therefore, one must practice authentically and realize authentically;
one must plant both feet firmly on the ground before it can be attained. One must obtain the official certificate of the Way in hand before it can be attained.
If you have truly obtained it in hand, from that point on it is no longer a matter of concern; passing through the barriers and the checkpoints, the breast is cleared of all obstructions.

He strides across the ground with arms swinging, entirely without hesitation or inhibition. If you have not yet attained mastery, as soon as you reach a checkpoint or a frontier, your mind will inevitably feel uneasy.
Even if you stubbornly ignore it and stumble blindly past, once you have passed through the gateway, [the consequences remain].
Suddenly, if someone were to say "Kiai" (the sound of striking the meditation seat), you would immediately turn red-faced;
you would be caught by others, and this failure would not be a minor matter. It is just like those of you in this assembly:

if you could distinguish yourself by obtaining a thousand or ten thousand coins to purchase a genuine *duce* (ordination certificate) and tuck it into your bosom, you could then travel everywhere as a wandering monk.
Whether staying alone or joining a community, you must remain free and at ease.

If your place of origin is not clear and your realization is not authentic, you are merely seeking unhappiness for yourself. As soon as you step through the gate, you will be pointed out by others as a man who is "not up to it.
Do not let it happen that you further encounter someone ill-suited to you, who will twist you around until you have no defense.
The moment you grasp at it, you become flustered and confused; it would be better to be a common man from a village of three households who has passed away, for he has none of these many affairs.

Therefore, I told you earlier that you must have both feet firmly planted on the ground before you can succeed, and that you must first obtain the official certificate of the Way. Even when you reach such a state, you still cannot yet—
Stop. Have you not seen the Way of the ancients? To practice Chan, one must attain awakening; having attained awakening, one must encounter a person.

If one does not encounter such a person, ten out of every five or two will be mere fabrications. It is truly so. First, one must not carry a wooden board upon one’s shoulders and rely on it for self-assurance;

rather, one must abandon what is short and follow what is long, seeking decisive discernment from others. Within this gate of mine, there are a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions, with hidden and manifest aspects that are utterly distinct.
On this path, none can know it except those with great wisdom and penetrating clarity. Have you not seen how Muping visited Luopu? He posed a question, saying:
"What is it like before the single bubble has arisen? Luopu replied: "Shift the boat and you will understand the currents; raise the oars and you will distinguish the waves.
Muping did not find resonance there, so he went instead to ask Panlong: "What is it like before the single bubble has arisen? Long—
It is said: "When moving the boat, one does not part from the water; yet as soon as the oars are raised, the source is lost. Upon hearing this, Muping attained enlightenment.
Later, Master Yunfeng Yue took up this case and remarked: "If Muping had attained enlightenment under Luopo’s words, he would still have been somewhat better off.
Later, however, he was not right; he ended up being drowned in the stagnant waters of Panlong. After Yunfeng established his own monastery, someone asked him: "What is Muping?"
Píng said, "No need for the axe. Indeed, he simply sat right there. You tell me: what was the intent behind his speaking thus?
Many of you brothers often deliberate, saying, "If one moves the boat, one leaves the water;
if one raises the oar, one loses the source"—this is merely dead water. What is Mùpíng? "No need for the axe. This is why he simply sat.
In this regard, if you understand it in such a way, you will not have even dreamed of it for donkey years.

Here, you must see through that single point where the ancients were loathed by others before you can succeed. Furthermore, did you not see how Chan Master Ning of Fuyong visited Grand Master Shixing?
When the Grand Master ascended the hall, he took his staff in his right hand, placed it on his left side, and said:
Had it not been for Brother Fuyong, this matter would have remained difficult to fully comprehend. He then descended from the seat. Later, Huanglong took up the case and said:
"Master Shixing could not even bring himself to stop; instead, he used the Buddha-dharma to cater to human sentiment.
To this day, beneath ten thousand ages, he serves as a source of laughter for people. Now tell me: when Huanglong spoke thus, did he approve of him or not?"
He has come here. If he is merely one who has attained "radish-head Chan," I fear he will not be able to comprehend it.

Therefore, since you have already entered the gate of Chan meditation, you must also attain its conclusion; only then will you be free from doubt regarding the tongues of all the old masters of the world.
If you truly have no point of entry yet, you must treat this as the most urgent matter.
One must first comprehend the single most essential matter. The ancients possessed great skillful means to lead you onto the path;
you must therefore, day and night—three times each—take up a single "capping phrase" (huatou) that cannot be bitten through.

In the midst of a cold, indifferent state, bite it here and there until, suddenly, by a slip of the tongue, you bite through it. Then, laugh to yourself once, and thereafter, establish yourself firmly upon this very ground.
Come! You have truly displayed a remarkable character. Furthermore, I have one more matter to inform you, brothers:
by no means should you create difficulties for yourselves by first becoming discouraged. As soon as you entertain such a view, there will never be a time when you attain anything.
Nevertheless, you must also apply some measure of discernment; if you are of keen capacity, you will penetrate it at a single glance, and naturally, you will not die.
At the end of the passage, he recalls an ancient saying: "I have a phrase; I will tell it to you when a calf gives birth to a calf.
He further says: "I have a phrase; I will tell it to you when the waters of a cave stream flow uphill. And he says again:
I have a single phrase; I will speak it to you only when the mountain stump falls over on its side.
At this point, even those with eyes wide open would be bewildered. Do not take offense, for today this old monk shall once more provide you with a thread of guidance.
I have a single phrase; I have already spoken it to all of you before ever reaching Jiaoshan. It is simply that you yourselves—
"You should have avoided it. Although this is so, can you truly avoid it? [The Master] strikes the meditation seat and descends.

Tonight’s general discourse is due to the request of the Great Master, intended to offer memorial services for Consort Chen, the late Lady Shufei, desiring to establish the causal conditions of Prajñā to provide merit for her posthumous peace, and furthermore, to bring enlightenment to all people.
The mind of the Way is indeed extraordinary; it is indeed vast and great. I, this mountain monk, have seldom engaged in general expositions (pǔshuō).
This is because my lifelong speech has been dull and my nature lacks the capacity for retention. Now, a general exposition must possess a broad dharma-nature and expansive waves;
it must belong to those predecessors such as Dazhu, Nanyang, Deshan, Linji, Yantou, Luoshan, and later Yuanwu and Dahui.
Wisdom and the response from the hermitage are both scarce these days. Nevertheless, the clouds and moon are the same, yet the streams and mountains differ.

Generally speaking, those of great capacity have their own livelihood, and those of lesser capacity have their own means of subsistence. Yet, though one may explain it a thousand times or ten thousand ways, in the end, it remains merely an explanation.
This matter does not reside in the place of explanation; rather, within the sphere of each person, it stands as a solitary wall of ten thousand feet.
It is simply a matter of sitting and cutting off all confusion; there has never been anything that is "not this" or "this.

It is only because practitioners among you have arbitrarily created complications and arbitrarily fabricated contrivances within it that they create obstacles for themselves, leading to a state where they cannot make use of it.

It is evident that here, not even a single point of external calculation can be applied. As soon as one involves even a hair’s breadth of external calculation, it becomes a superfluous teaching. Why? Because...
The alms bowl has a handle; thus, when it moves, its shadow appears, and when one awakens, ice forms.
Even if you remain unmoving and unawakened, you are sitting directly upon a place where death is certain. At this point, how can you realize it? How can you settle into it?
How can you attain resonance with this matter? You must achieve a state where your entire body breaks into a sweat from within your own cold ground.

It is only upon one instance of losing your laugh that you will attain it. If you have not yet experienced such a moment, then no matter how flawlessly you may explain it—like a vessel that does not leak water—it will merely result in an external circumlocution and only add to a scene of clamor;
it simply has no connection whatsoever to this matter. Have you not seen the Patriarch Baiyun say: "If you can attain the true and authentic..."?
When you break into a sweat and emerge, a jade palace and a crystal hall will appear upon a single blade of grass.
If you have not yet broken into a sweat once, even if there were jade palaces and crystal halls, they would be covered over by that single blade of grass. Truly, these words are right;
it could be said: "A blow from a staff strikes the head of a stone man. Stripping away all layers to discuss the actual reality—if you truly step upon this...
My son, naturally there is no such turmoil; it is simply a state of being vast and at ease.
Yet, when suddenly pressed by others, fire breaks out from beneath the water; what is grasped is immediately employed, each instance covering heaven and earth.
In reality, there is nothing else: everywhere is entirely one's own. There is no need for contrivance or calculation; therefore, without moving a single thing—
Dust. Without wavering from a single point, upon seeing the matter, one immediately speaks the answer; the Elder’s foot finds no entry.
These are all words spoken by predecessors who have seen through to the very top and bottom, with not a single thread of leakage remaining.
How could those of shallow caliber possibly be compared to them? As for this place, Nanyue (Rurong), there is truly nothing [to be grasped].

Chan is for people; humaneness is for people; the Way is for people to study. It is simply this matter of putting on clothes, eating food, defecating, urinating, and being an unintelligent fellow—a patch-robed monk from the vast seas—who, despite being so, has not been shunned by you great masters as you come here to this solitary peak and summit to together maintain a life of austerity.
Therefore, I do not dare to treat my brothers lightly in ordinary matters. Friends, all...
Whenever the fifth day arrives, I must ascend the hall; on the third and eighth days, I must post the notice board.
I do this merely to fulfill my duty as abbot, neither out of pride in my scholarly understanding nor to dazzle others with my insights, nor to concoct strange and fabricated tales.
I simply rely on what I have personally seen and meet with you, my brothers, in a state of bare-bones nakedness. Yet, when you brothers enter the room, you must reveal that which...
As for those who have received the transmission, it cannot be said that they are entirely non-existent; there are many who walk upon the true path.
As soon as I see a brother walking upon the true path, I do not dare to let him pass lightly by; instead, I descend the steps and lead him along for a step or two.
As soon as one reaches the point of letting go, yet again one cannot proceed further. In truth, there is nothing else;
it is simply because one has never once broken into a genuine sweat. However, this single resolution cannot be contrived, nor can it be calculated.
If one is of keen capacity, a single bite severs it, and a single glance penetrates through it, leaving no room for such hesitations. If, however, one relies on intellectual ingenuity...
Even if you are dull-witted, you must not let yourself off lightly; you must instead make your resolve firm and certain, advancing with courageous vigor.
Unshaken by any circumstance and unswayed by any words, remain like one who has entered a land of lethal poisons, where not even a single drop of water may touch them.
Stand upright like a cliff rising ten thousand fathoms, remaining unchanged from beginning to end.

Suddenly, with a slip of hand and a stumble of foot, one sees oneself topple over; only then does one cease to be deceived by others, and only then can one avoid betraying the original vow of one’s pilgrimage.
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, one will have no fear of that fellow from the House of Yama.
Furthermore, consider Master Yin: although she was a nun, she possessed the deeds of a true man. To examine the reason for this, she followed...

Coming from a life of wealth and honor, he left the home-life for a true reason; he traveled on pilgrimage for a true reason; he met spiritual friends for a true reason; and he studied the Way for a true reason.
Because his causal ground was correct from the beginning, he remained unerring from start to finish; thus, he has not failed himself.
On the night of the twenty-eighth day of the tenth month last year, he suddenly reached out his hand and touched his own nostrils, and thereby came to know that all along—
With his great head hanging down, he came straight to the abbot’s quarters to explain his reason for being there. At that time, I regretted not giving him a severe beating.
I imagine that even now he would still long to receive one; however, my staff is currently not here, so I shall wait for another day to hand it over.
Once I have obtained its handle in my hand, it will be the perfect opportunity to let go of my clouds and descend to meet people.
Winnowing. Inside the Buddha Hall, the Yellow-Faced Old Man is currently engaged in Zen meditation. As the saying goes: "Coarse food satisfies easily; fine chewing leads to hunger.
Nowadays, those who take coarse food are many, while those who practice fine chewing are few. Today, I shall open it up for you and speak further.
Now is the very time when it is appropriate to step forward and investigate, or to step back and investigate. It is like milk...
Elder Feng is truly laughable. He tells people to come forward and investigate, and then he tells them to step back and investigate.
What kind of talk is this? A person who has attained it will surely nod their head in secret.
The other day, having first received a bit of news, he was filled with boundless joy and immediately began to assert himself, refusing to admit that anything was not right. Now...
When you come here, simply set everything down and listen to what others say. However, in the practice of Chan, one must never carry a "one-sided board.
If you do not carry such a board, then from the winter solstice night until New Year’s morning, there will still be a great deal of snow ahead.
As soon as you carry that board, you have already lost the world, for you lack the primary hand. When I was in the assembly practicing Chan in years past, I...
I know for myself that I possess only the strength of one who does not carry a single-sided board. Although I do not hope to equal the ancients today, I nonetheless have a modicum of shame.
In the past, when Old Dongshan had attained Zen, there were people at that time who did not approve of him;
yet when someone went to challenge him, he would respond appropriately. It is actually you all who have fully mastered this.
The Master speaks. When I see the Master, I only recognize my own shame. These two characters, "recognizing shame"—you are truly soft-headed and stubborn.
Whether among the masters of past and present or the monks of the world, none have reached it; all fail to emerge from his domain.

Clearly, this matter must involve a sense of shame before it can be attained. If you lack a sense of shame, then even if you have investigated thoroughly and reached awakening, you are merely a "Chan scholar.
As soon as you are seen by one with clear eyes, you will only become an object of ridicule.
Now tell me, does Nanyang Huichao feel any shame in speaking thus? I also wish for everyone to examine and scrutinize this. Furthermore, I shall offer another verse to the assembly:
The Great Master Kaihua said: "The primary cause comes to travel on pilgrimage; A single phrase upon crossing the gate."
Casually treading upon it, the hairless lock is opened and the cordless bond is untied. Upon the summit of Mount Moshan, one lets loose their folly:
the ox-head faces north, the horse-head faces south.
An Ancient Case:

When the World-Honored One ascended the seat and the assembly had just gathered, Kāśyapa struck the gavel and said, "The World-Honored One has finished preaching the Dharma. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat.
The Master said: "What the World-Honored One spoke constitutes only the Introductory Section (Nidāna). What Kāśyapa spoke constitutes only the Dissemination Section (Pravartana).
As for the Main Section (Śarīra), it has never been touched upon. Tonight, Jing Mountain will expound it without sparing his eyebrows.
He took up his staff, struck the ground once, and said: "Do you understand? The three sections are distinct; they are all gathered back into the preceding category. Furthermore...
*Claps the desk once.* After the World-Honored One had entered Parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa arrived later. When the outer coffin was opened, his twin feet were revealed.
The Master addressed the great assembly, saying: "Of the hundreds of thousands who gathered at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, only Kāśyapa alone succeeded to the Patriarchal seat. Truly..."
How shameful! Why? Because he personally saw the heels of the Yellow-Faced Old Man.
When the World-Honored One saw Mañjuśrī standing outside the gate, he said, "Mañjuśrī, why do you not enter the gate?"
Mañjuśrī said, "I do not see a single dharma outside the gate.
The Master said, "To explain such extraordinary principles is indeed worthy of him, the Teacher of the Seven Buddhas; yet, when examined closely, he cannot be let off so easily.
At that time, had Mañjuśrī responded in this manner, the Master would have followed up by saying to him, "Stay outside the gate for now. If...
If you can penetrate this point, you may allow that woman to emerge from her confinement.
Master Fu Dashi said: "Crowned and wearing a patched robe, with Confucian shoes, he paid court to Emperor Wu of Liang.
