Tie of Fenghua was loathed by some and feared by others. He was not a man from Mingzhou; he must have been from Su[zhou].
The local dialect says:

At the place where Dongshan said there were "ten thousand miles of no inch of grass," one goes to where the flat ground reveals human corpses. The hermitage master takes his own body and buries it in one spot; the scattered skulls lie piled upon one another.
Relying on this, the mournful winds and sorrowful mists cannot overcome my longing.
Great Following covers the tortoise bone with skin; skin wraps the bone. Great Following releases the soaring falcon of the distant heavens; east, west, south, and north, it raises its wings in vain.
Mou did not realize they had already passed through the kingdom of Silla.
Attendant Kuò asked Dēshān, "Where have all the sages of antiquity gone? [Dēshān replied:
"A stubborn-skinned tiger lies on a forest mound; let passersby do as they please, dripping oil upon it. Its belly is full only because it has once been satiated."
Flesh. Even if one calls out to it repeatedly, it is too lazy to raise its head.
Rockhead’s arising and ceasing never stop;
arising and ceasing never stop—who understands how to look? When pressed at the critical moment, one penetrates the heavy barrier; east and west are both Chang’an.
The Way is vast and open; moving freely without constraint, one comes and goes.
A monk asked Shishuang, "Within the span of a few feet, why do I not behold the Master’s countenance? Shishuang replied:
"My Way pervades the entire realm and has never been hidden," [said Shishuang]. Later, a monk asked Xuefeng, "What is the meaning of 'pervading the entire realm and never being hidden'?
Xuefeng said, "Where is it not Shishuang? The monk returned and related this to Shishuang.
Shishuang said, "Why is this old fellow in such a hurry to die? [Later,] Xuansha said, "On the mountain peak."
The old man has missed his way,
yet we share the springtime of Dongting Lake from the same boat. All day long he lingers in the shade of the willow-lined shore,
until a fisherman adds his oars and sweeps him effortlessly across the heart of the azure waves.
Dizang plows his fields to earn a meal (2):
A single piece of uncut jade from Mount Jing—those who can clearly discern it are rare. How many cast a furtive glance, yet view it as nothing more than a common stone?
Plowing the fields for a broad meal, lying full and stretching out one's legs; were the three realms brought here, they would be placed on the left side.
This drew forth the old, ancient fellow Longya, who held in his hand a broken wooden ladle.
The State Preceptor called the attendant three times;
with one toss of the divine cup, he determined fortune and misfortune. Re-examining and divining again, his spiritual penetration became even more profound.
Having clearly perceived the events of this year, he spoke of how the affairs of next year would be different.

Jianyuan, consoling the deceased, dreamed of returning home and asked about his native land. Clearly the answer was given, yet he still feigned madness. When the white clouds had vanished, he turned his head back once more;
boundless green mountains face the setting sun.
Panshan heard the song:
"The red wheel is certain to sink in the west; I wonder to which direction the soul shall go? With one cry of wailing, there is nowhere to hide;
lifting the head, one personally sees one's own father and mother."
A monk asked Chan Master Tianzhang Baoyue, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
Tianzhang said, "There are three hundred and sixty days in a year. The monk asked, "If one proceeds in this very manner, what then? Tianzhang said, "Ten thousand miles away is not yet far."
In a year of three hundred and sixty days, day after day the sun rises from the eastern side; last night at dusk it again set in the west.
Vast and boundless, there is nowhere to find its traces.

The old man Hào wears coarse cloth trousers and a collar, yet he boasts of wealth and status; he sells his own poverty for a pittance. While murder may be forgiven, such lack of propriety is unforgivable.
A monk asked Master Cizhao of Guyin, "What is the Way? Zhao replied, "The third day of the twelfth month."
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, opening one’s mouth is already an imperial edict; if you intend to ask further, “How is it?
by the first day of the first month tomorrow, the monk asked an ancient worthy, “What is the Master’s profound and subtle place? The ancient worthy descended [into silence].
On the meditation seat, he performs a woman’s bow and says, "Thank you for coming from afar; there is nothing with which to receive you.
He bows deeply and personally, encompassing the full rites of three generations. If this meaning were not so, would it be merely about jade and silk?
"Are the wheat ripening before the mountains yet?

The great artisan does not strive for cleverness; the great scholar does not rely on study. Every movement spontaneously accords with the square and the circle; everything raised becomes ritual and music.
How laughable are those diviners in the countryside, who labor in vain to bore through the shell of a tortoise."
Among humans, there is no water that does not flow toward the east. Why, then, does the Yellow River flow northward?
Dark and dim is the sandbar; dark and dim is the sandbar. Of ten ships that come, nine are overturned. Only Chan Shangshe of the Three Mountains remains.
I walk toward the land. Look! What can you do to me?
A monk asked Dàlóng: "The physical body decays;
mountain flowers are like brocade, the water is like indigo. Suddenly emerging from heaven and earth, his countenance is not revealed. He once trod by the banks of the Wǔlíng Stream."
The road leads into a cavern where the spring colors differ from those of the human world;
in verse,
the blossoming light of ten plum trees.
Letting go from the precipice—casting oneself off from the top of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff. Only then does one know that the blossoming of flowers has no concern for spring.
To seek further branches and leaves from this very place would make one laugh out loud at the man beneath the tree of old.

Having passed away and revived once more, the solitary root has shed its husk and lies upon the verdant moss. In the cold stillness, for no apparent reason, the eyes of laughter open. Do not be surprised that snow and frost cannot deceive it;
it is simply because it has already come from the midst of death.
On level ground, spring returns;
ten thousand trees and a thousand flowers remain unawakened from the frost. Nowhere can the Lord of the East find his way back. Raising my eyes, I suddenly behold the face of the spring breeze:
vivid and bright upon the branches are a few specks of green.
Within the plain there is flavor;
half-open and half-closed, beyond flourishing and withering. Seeming to exist yet seeming not to exist, within this leisurely detachment, there is a unique and singular air.
I laugh at those reds and purples vying for fragrance amidst the thickets.
A branch extends out horizontally;

do not say that only the southern branch can release its flowers. The northern beauty branching alongside is also worthy of praise. There is no need to contend over high or low among the yellow plums;
the grasses and trees transmitted from the past belong to one single family.
Five leaves joined in fragrance;
the flowers bloom in five petals, naturally fragrant. Outshining musk and outshining orchids, it possesses a distinct scent. Having transmitted the spiritual root, it remains eternally imperishable;
how could it merely linger in the radiance of its blossoms?
In the blossoming and closing of flowers, there is both correctness and partiality; where things are incomplete, they become complete. One must know from what root and stem this is obtained;
for the most part, it is seen to grow buried by the edge of a cave stream.
High and low according to suitability;
trees have heights and branches have lengths. Wherever flowers bloom, they fit perfectly. It is all because one has skillfully grasped the essence of the tip of a hair;
whether vertical strokes or horizontal sweeps, none are obstructed.

When illusory flowers wither away, their petals and branches—those to the north and those to the south—face one another, lean, or slant in all such ways. What need is there to wait for Zhi Lang to laboriously sketch them?
Behold them as they bloom, and see them as they fade.
The true mark is eternally perfect:
a yellow base is naturally yellow, a blue base is blue. At the tip of every branch, one sees the Heavenly Truth.
Now, having forgotten all its bitterness and astringency, how can the seed-kernel be shown to others?
The morning sun pierces through a tattered robe, with pieces joined haphazardly, some long and some short, stitched together as chance dictates. One merely sees the sun rising in the east;
one knows not what year it is in this dusty world.
Facing the moon, you finish reading the sutras;
entering the sea to count its sands, you merely exhaust yourself in vain. Before the wind and beneath the moon, how many times have you knit your brows? If you would rest now, then rest;
if you seek the moment of completion, there is no time of completion.
Having entered, he closed it again;
after passing through several clouds and mists in the south, he gathered rare and precious goods that filled his ship.
With a snap of his fingers, the wind-swept sails reached the shore, and everything was instantly transformed into great radiant coins.
Mourning the past, the empty mountains are vast and silent; yellow leaves fall with a whistling sound. This person does not come, so I wait for them through the evening until the dawn.
If this person were to come, we would both remain speechless and our longing would dissolve. Return now! My robes flutter, the road stretches far and long—who is there to share it?
That solitary peak stands like the moon in the azure sky.
As he walks among the mountains in the four dignified postures, he moves his steps with such lightness as if to avoid startling the hidden birds; there is no other intent behind this.
Dwelling in the mountains, one does not know the number of fallen leaves; no one sweeps them, and they obscure the path to the pine gate.
Sitting in the mountains, one becomes indolent through the practice of leisure; offering few flowers, one sees only monkeys stealing fruit.
Lying in the mountains, I was unaware that the seasons had passed. Rain beat against the window, utterly shattering my fine dreams.
Next, following the rhyme of Zhao Longtu’s "Thundering Sound Hall" on the Kaifeng Prefectural Governor of Jiankang:
"In the clear sky, thunder crashes; there is nothing to pursue. Those who hear it must be made mute by those who discern it. Seizing the boundaries of the realm, one acts with rectitude."
The command: To soar far beyond past, present, and future—this matter is luminously clear;
there is no need to seek it. Though one possesses a mouth all over the body, one remains as mute as a mute. I laugh at Old Lu for being so busy (the words of Longtu);
he draws out vines and pulls at branches, deceiving the ancients and the moderns alike.

The gate of the layman stands tens of thousands of fathoms high; once I heard a single word that awakened the blind and the mute. Who would have known that the principle of "the same breeze blowing across a thousand li" was so vividly and clearly manifest before my very eyes this very day?
Next, the Preface by Editor Zou, Governor of Pingjiang:
The "Broad Way" (Bodao) person came from the Western Capital carrying a ladle of foul water to splash the old monk.
I, Yuyang, borrowed his handle and splashed him twice in return. Since he is one who walks the Path, he surely will not harbor ill will.
At Caoxi, wind and waves arise from level ground; in later generations, as the boat rises, the water rises too. I send word to those who drift with the current:
you must cast away the oar in your hands.
Once you piloted an iron boat through the surging ocean waves; surely you had no fear of the towering crests.
Now, not a single drop remains in the Qinyang River—do not recklessly inquire how deep it is with your oar.
Next, in the rhyme of the farewell for Chief Seat Huì by Zhao, the Prefect of Changsha:
Traveling on foot, you have personally reached the very source; I know for certain this was no ordinary journey.
When you return, if anyone asks for news of Wufeng, Tell them that at Longyuan, the stream has already ceased to flow.
Who can understand this verse of severing the stream? Only the ancient master of Vaiśālī. This is not like hoping for plums to quench one's thirst;
the soup has already been prepared on the southern branches.
In the same rhyme, a verse for the stupa of Chan Master Chang of Damei:

At the place where Master Ma questioned him, there was no trace left behind; Sometimes he spoke of the three winters, sometimes of the nine autumns. If you recognize it, the mind is itself the Buddha;
A single strand of hair is just a single strand of hair.
Vast and boundless, they pluck leaves and seek branches; To the mountain elder alone, I grant the direct vision of Him.
A single stroke, and one travels thirty thousand miles; To this day, few know His footprints.
Viewing life and death as a playground—truly one knows that Laozi has never perished. Where may one now inquire after his news?
The wind carries the fragrance of plum blossoms, striking the bridge of the nose.
Sent to Master Yan Shi of Yunju:
At Vulture Peak the clouds disperse and the frosty sky is cold; North, south, east, and west, a single moon hangs solitary.
I am glad to receive this good news from the rivers and lakes: Master Dianxiong is at Yunju.
How many times have I dreamed of the heights of white clouds? I wish to go, yet am held back by the pull of sloth and illness.
On what day shall we lean upon one another through the pouring night, When the moon is cold over a thousand ridges and a single cry of a monkey rings out?
From the beginning, one has had a mouth hanging on a blank wall; who would believe that now even the mouth is gone?
Because I recall the guest whose entire body was raw and festering, there was no reason for this white paper to be needlessly smeared over.
The Shaoshi Peak is shrouded in dust, its empty walls cold and desolate. I am not yet weary of my family’s tradition of profound stillness. Outside the gate, as before, deep snow accumulates;
I know not who would be willing to stand with their waist buried in it.
Master Zhi says:
"The myriad dharmas all return to the One Dharma; yet one does not know where that One Dharma returns to. When hungry, buy a sesame cake and eat it;
having eaten the sesame cake, the belly is no longer hungry."
Stones and weeds fall in profusion; mostly they compete for the rich soil. Truly, who is able to strike a single blow with the hoe?
How many times have we seen the sprouts emerge only to retreat in shame? It is simply because there is nowhere to apply one's effort.
Beyond the eastern mouth of the river, to the west of the East Sea and south of the West Sea, the reeds sway and the waters stretch vast and wide. Even Master Xie does not yet know its location;
do not regard it as an ordinary islet or sandbar.
On the high plateau where Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot look up, a single thread of light secretly penetrates—how deep it is! Severe as ice and cold as snow, no one understands;
it pours empty down the broken cliff for thousands of fathoms.

The old man was startled by the drum smeared with lethal poison; had he not escaped, his entire body would have perished. Who would believe that beneath a skull, a beard could grow anew from the jaw? *Fuguku* (Restoring the Ancient).
The wheat has already appeared and the rice fills the fields; with baskets for frames and drums of earth, the music is harmonious and serene.
One might not know it were the age of the Yellow Emperor, but it is truly the year of Treasure Prosperity opened by Heaven.
The clouds and valleys sometimes contract and sometimes expand, manifesting many transformations; responding immediately to every call, they reveal the innate truth.
Who would have known that where the path turns and the peaks bend back, the warbling of a secluded bird amidst the fragrant blossoms is a spring all its own?

A withered tree does not fall into the hands of a woodcutter; it does not enter the gate of a master carver from Ying. Thus, it grows old in the hills and valleys, yet remains free from the marks of axe and hatchet.
Boundless.
Staggering and yet staggering; level and even, more level and even. Reaching out one’s hand, one cannot see one’s own palm. Zhaozhou’s East Courtyard and West Courtyard.
Nantang and Deshan return speechless to their quarters. Xianggu bends his head and enters the thatched hut. A great eagle soars ninety thousand li in a single bound.
In the village, by the hedge, the swallows and sparrows chirp in vain.
Splashing about, they scratch their heads, forgetting where the itch lies;
they toy with things without knowing their names. There is one thing that remains unclarified—something that cannot be purchased even for a thousand pieces of gold.
Constantly aware that for even a moment to be absent is the same as death; though thoroughly awake, one still deceives oneself.
One long cherished the old woman of the eastern village, who, upon meeting a monk, would also know how to say "namo."

The zither-rest is ingeniously fashioned in the likeness of a charred paulownia tree; it contains the pure tones of antiquity. Often one listens to it while harmonizing with dreams, yet it merely joins the chirping of nocturnal insects.
— By Bōwō (Limping Old Man)
In ordinary walking, one does not fall into the ordinary. Everyone speaks of the length of the feet; who knows the shortness of the feet?
This stinking hut is utterly devoid of breath, yet it truly permeates others. Only those without nostrils are fit to be its neighbors.
Next, Master Yanyun of Nanzhan, following the rhyme of Xuedou’s “Jinjing,” writes:

The myriad phenomena merge into a single mirror-case; even the nine colors are not yet many. Perfect purity produces an excellent model; the woven pattern requires no clever shuttle. It has a form that cannot be manufactured;
being traceless, what need is there for polishing? I ask: when light and shadow have vanished, how can it be otherwise? How can it be otherwise?
Seeing off Zhao Longtu as he returns to Siming:
In years past, we once made a pact to return to Siming, To join our bowls and share a meal of *pú* greens and broth. The mustard greens in the eastern garden have withered and grown again;
How could I, Wangzhi, fail to honor this vow? Why should one be bound by such petty, tinkling virtues? A great name ought to be made resoundingly known.

Magnificent! Your banners and standards remain motionless as you exterminate the Hu tribes; with a single stretch of an arm, you surpass the Great Wall. Once the lands of Huai are pacified, the four seas are at peace.
Your abundant achievements and sublime virtue would be difficult to name. You clearly understand that the eight delicacies are equal to wild herbs and potherbs;

for you, leisure and nobility are but the same. I am afflicted by the fires of the kalpa, yet I remain truly unperturbed; you regard the "day-garment" (the honor of returning home) not as a source of glory. The Seven Buddhas...
Succession upon succession—what basis is there for it? The Sixth Patriarch’s incessant clamor is but the empty sound of a bowl. Have you not seen the iron dragon-head atop the bannerpole?
A goose feather is exceedingly heavy; mountains and peaks are light. (The Sixth Patriarch and the Seven Buddhas are the words of Longtu.)

Seeing off Master Wuxiang as he returns to his hometown: same name, same title, same native roots. Dwelling together upon the rivers and lakes, there is no distinction between self and other. Sometimes we ascend together to the peak of a solitary mountain;

sometimes we descend together to the bottom of the vast ocean. We share in suffering and grieve together; we rejoice in joy and delight together. Gold is joined with gold, and water is cleansed by water.
Water. Sometimes it twists and turns its iron face; heart and mouth are entirely at odds.
If you stay, I go; if you go, I stop. Amidst the bright sun and blue sky, thunder and lightning roar;
on level ground where there is no wind, waves arise. It is not non-being; it is being. West River Daisui; Tongcheng Touzi.

Seeing off Master Netang as he takes up residence at Tianning Monastery in Xiu—Suzhou has it, Changzhou has it, the Real has it, yet it has never existed. When one is lowly, the whole kingdom cannot be exchanged for it;
when one is noble, one must pay money to buy a single peck. Stretching out one hand and pulling back the other, days and months race by in haste, while mountains and rivers run backward.
The blind donkey of Jibei takes three steps back; the lame-footed Yunmen opens his mouth wide. Aha-ha!
This story is already widely circulated now; why wait for thirty years later?
Sending off Master Shu’ān as he takes up residence at Yunju:
The waters of Donghu Lake are deep, coiling with an ancient dragon. Morning and evening it appears and disappears without a fixed trace; opening its mouth or closing it, it spews fragrant mists;
lifting its feet or setting them down, it stirs a chilling wind from below. Now he departs for his new home at Yunju; his majestic spirit resounds through ten thousand apertures.
He cried out in indignation, saying: "This is not the man who plucked the pearl; you should not have lightly trodden the path to Mount Ou-feng.
He escorted the Abbot Ning back to Shu.
For five years we lived together in adversity; though I had already nodded my head in agreement, you likewise did not grant your consent. Among these matters—
I cannot bear it. To break off the exposed pillar of clarity—such clumsy conduct is truly unforgivable.
Amidst the whistling winds and dewy cold of the ninth month, you suddenly come to bid farewell and return to your home. At the parting of the ways, you are utterly senseless;
yet you insist on seeking a turning phrase from me. How can one utter such a turning phrase? It is like wrapping a tiger in wet paper, or striking it with a heavy club.
The rat. Aha ha! There is no place for you to find it.
I send this to Chan Master Tanzang at Xuefeng to see Chijue (formerly of Fulong).
In this world, all snakes may be toyed with, but the "tortoise-nose" of Nanshan must not be moved. To move it is to touch its cold mouth and suffer a hidden wound.
A person who wounds another to the point of death does not know the pain [of being wounded]. You are now leaving; you should take care of yourself.
If in the future you encounter a mouthful of poison and return, do not say that this mountain monk did not tell you.
Seeing off My Younger Brother, the Venerable Shao, as he returns to his native land:
What is this "shining and brilliant" thing? It is neither a thing, nor a mind, nor even a Buddha. Yet those in the five lakes, clad in cloud-like robes, vie with one another to seek it;
they vainly waste their time and energy in oblivion. I have wandered through the rivers and lakes for thirty-four years, eating my fill of rice.
The rest is merely idling away time in sleep. My son now wanders far and wide in bitter searching; I do not know what he seeks or what he yearns for.
When asked about my Way, this year’s harvest is bountiful and the reaping is early. When asked about my Chan, the autumn forest is full of chirping, its evening sounds a clamorous din.
I have shaken out my guts and entrails and spoken it all; do not take even a single word back with you. It would be too easy for it to flow abroad in vain.
These words, once written down, become divergent and separate. My gaze reaches the home mountains where clouds pile upon one another; I too wish to return, yet I cannot.
For a thousand miles and ten thousand leagues, there is but a single iron bar.

The man of the forest and springs finds joy in the forest and springs; having attained the true essence of the forest and springs, when thirsty he scoops up the spring water to drink, and when vigorous he penetrates the woods to go forth.

How often does one see the warbling of solitary birds? Yellow leaves gather as incense drifts in; the snow falls like flying cotton—throughout the four seasons, all is suited to my heart’s desire. Ten thousand...
The elephant is my companion. When someone asked further what his intention was, he laughed and pointed to the great pine tree before the cliff.
A-he-he! How joyful! How joyful! What is there to be sought?

Re-casting the rice-pot, one fails to realize that it has been extensively encrusted with rust; with a single blow it is shattered and cast anew. In this ordinary act, the body is liberated from its old molds;
yet when the porridge is cooked as before, it is no longer the same soup.
The Great Lotus receives guests;
where can one seek the traces of those who come from the waters and clouds? Having trampled through the peaks of Tiantai and Yanfang, when physical strength is exhausted, the true message remains.
The Little Lotus receives the Great Lotus.
In Ninghai, where the smoke and waves reach their end, fertile fields stretch wide; when paths are exhausted, a new livelihood begins.
North and south, travelers bustle about—truly many are these scholars—but who among them can be called a person of "sufficient realization"?
When the cock crows, one receives guests;
meeting water and clouds at night, one must seek lodging. Once the meal is finished, what hinders proceeding further? Does the master of the mountain merely open his gates for hospitality?
His purpose in raising a cock is for its crowing at the fifth watch.
The former Daoist (formerly the Abbot of Yulong), clad in yellow robes, has abandoned them to mingle with those in black.
He has cast aside the sweet peach to pluck the sour pear; having tasted both their bitterness and astringency all at once, he returns with furrowed brows—whom will he find who understands?
The Daoist Master Jing says:
"Our heads and brains are not alike, yet our nostrils have always been the same.
Feeling it myself in this cool place, I see that the Old Lord originally wore a cap of mulberry bark."

The physiognomist [sees] a block of weathered, gnarled, rotten, and withered firewood. How many times has he seen the spring breeze grow green moss? Yet it is said that even this Master grants his approval;
in some distant year, the flowers will surely bloom.
The Way lies in the freedom from fixed forms;
where there is no confinement, how could one remain stagnant in a single place? Since every mountain possesses stone, one may carve a stele wherever one is.
Thus, I praise the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Śākyamuni went out from the mountains;
why did he enter them? What was his purpose in coming forth? Why did he depart? Had he known the affairs of today beforehand, he would have regretted not being more cautious at the beginning.
The Great Being Avalokiteśvara raises his rosary to display his skill; for no reason, he manifests the appearance of a child.
How could this compare to the moon shining bright as frost fills the heavens, where a solitary monkey’s cry pierces through the peaks?

Flowing with the stream, it flows into the stream; without discrimination, it is perfectly pervasive everywhere, leaking forth from every head. The clouds clear across the eight directions and the celestial expanse is vast;
amidst ten thousand acres of waves, there is but a single lotus leaf.
Quiescent extinction manifests before one, like the moon suspended in the sky; its divided bodies benefit all beings, their reflections contained within the hundred rivers.

This is what is called "so being though not so," empty yet pervasive, still yet responsive. The springtime radiance of ten thousand lands, the moon’s reflection in a thousand rivers—where can it be sought now?
A single sound from the Universal Gate: a crane calls atop the cold pine summit.
How great is Avalokiteśvara! He skillfully observes all sounds, yet regarding these sounds, he does not form the view of them as "sound.
This very view is itself quiescent; there is no one who attains quiescence. By means of this, he is freed from all suffering and attains liberation everywhere.

He manifests emanations throughout the lands of the ten directions to rescue and deliver all beings; yet, within that act of rescuing and delivering, he harbors no thought of "rescuing and delivering."
It is like spring among the myriad flowers, making no distinction between long and short branches; or like the moon in the water, making no distinction between large and small vessels.
Responding to sounds and following what is contemplated, it impartially bestows benefit. These are the thirty-two manifestations and the fourteen fearlessnesses;
the gates of immeasurable skillful means are all fully accomplished. In each and every place of accomplishment, the very substance is like an illusion.
I contemplate her as having an illusory form; I vow to offer her an illusory praise. Should there be any who see or hear this, they should contemplate her in this way:

The fisherwoman Guanyin, with a body permeated by the stench of filth, is unaware of it herself as she comes again to the fish market to haggle for a bargain; among all that is alive therein, there are but few remaining.
"Son, who will you sell this to before the wind?
The fish in the basket, the pearls in the robe—seen being bought and sold, there is little reality and much falsehood.
Thus did the Great Being Mañjuśrī preach the Dharma for the Dragon Girl. (Praise requested by Chan Master Tai).
The Dharma of Mañjuśrī: what Dharma is it that he teaches? A woman attaining Buddhahood: what Buddha does she become? There is no dharma that can be taught;
there is no Buddha that can be attained. The dragon-king lies coiled yet exerts his power; the lion yawns and roars.
The three teachings merge to form a single face:
one-three-one-three and three-one-one-three. It cannot be dispersed by analysis, nor can it be gathered into a mass.
From ancient times to the present, they merge into a closed-mouthed face, simply because the gates and apertures are of many kinds.

The bodies of the sixteen arhats are like withered firewood; their minds are like precipitous cliffs. Though they possess ten thousand kinds of spiritual transformations, they maintain a single state of equanimity.
Looking at one another, they ultimately do not know the matter being discussed. On the following day, the Dragon King of Lake Anavatapta invited the Buddha for a midday meal.
Subhūti, with his white hair and missing teeth, was empty-minded and haughty within; yet he was struck down right before Kausika’s face and utterly humbled in the presence of Vimalakīrti.
Though he claimed to be foremost in understanding emptiness, he could do nothing but lean on his staff and brood in solitude.
Buddashu with chest bared and belly exposed, frowning and sticking out his chin, putting on such an act—what kind of ritual is this?
I say that he is not necessarily awake when you call him awake, nor does he necessarily sleep when you ask him to sleep. Hūṃ! Hūṃ! Son of Fenghua, I know you well.
The flesh weighs a thousand catties, yet there is not a grain of wisdom within. Turning his head and twisting his brain, he has obscured his own true nature.
This one spot is especially laughable: standing at the street corner waiting for someone. Had I seen him back then, I would have simply said slowly to him, "Thank you, Third Sister Silver-Scale."
Who cares about earth? Who cares about heaven? Drop the sackcloth bag and take a nap.
As for the future position of the successor, wait for donkey-year after donkey-year.

Wandering about to plunder cloth, he was both satiated and intoxicated, having no place for focused mindfulness; he let out a sneeze and further claimed it was the true Maitreya, clearly implying there must be another who is false.
The Layman Vimalakīrti feigned illness that has long been incurable; Mañjuśrī specifically applied the needle and the awl for him. The matter was stripped away with a single peck three feet long;
yet when questioned, he remained as before, like a drumstick.
Manifesting illness at Vaiśālī, he stirred wind and waves across level ground; no physician could find the source, for his ailment lay in his excessive speech.

Whether base or refined, coarse or fine, there is nothing that does not possess this quality. Pick up any single object, and it can both kill and give life.
Those who mistakenly ingest it often fall ill; yet this is not the fault of the medicine itself. Since Min is able to treasure it, [he shall surely succeed].
One should examine this with careful scrutiny.
Regarding the Dharma-talk of Master Dahui:
Master Dahui attained mastery over the Dharma; he was like the flow of a river from its source, its momentum descending naturally, vast and surging.
It is boundless. Sometimes it surges in anger; sometimes it breaks forth in flood; sometimes it is placid and still; sometimes it is violent and roars.

Its transformations are of myriad forms, yet from the beginning there is no intentional effort. When it reaches the sea, it blends into a single flavor, without the distinctions of rivers, springs, or flowing streams.
Asuras, mosquitoes, and gadflies drink according to their vessels, and all obtain full satisfaction. If one draws a ladleful from it...
This means exhausting the full extent of the great ocean. It is neither foolishness nor stupidity.
In the *Recorded Sayings of Yunke*, not long after Yunke entered nirvana, an unworthy son extracted the accounts of his lifelong failures and compiled them into one [work].

This great scroll is intended for circulation throughout all quarters, so as to unleash endless slander. For now, I have brought its substance to you, seeking your skillful investigation and verification.
I have therefore traced the origin of its words; they bear a resemblance to the compositions of the Right Ancestor (Huangbo) regarding the "Horizontal Cloth.
However, it is also full of errors at every turn and cannot be translated. Among it, there is one phrase that somewhat resembles the language of the Tang; if anyone can discern it—

Even were one to cut out one's own throat, it would not suffice to repay his kindness. Had there been even a moment’s hesitation, Qingliang would have gained the advantage of breathing through his nostrils.

In the *Record of the Iron Beak* (Tièzuì Yùlù), this old man is described as having nothing else of value throughout his life; he possessed only a single beak for the purpose of testing and examining those from all quarters. Thus, wherever he went, [he would... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the available portion while maintaining the technical terminology and classical style.)
At that time, no senior monks dared to confront his sharp edge. Consequently, his reputation as "Iron Beak" (Tièzuǐ) spread widely throughout the Jianghu region.
Later, he resided at the small monastery of Jīnzhi in Wumen, where he possessed the refined character and style of an ancient patriarch.

When students passed through his gate, some would test him by posing questions regarding the essential points of the separate transmission or the terminology of heterodox teachings; he would respond with verses immediately upon being questioned, like a valley echoing a sound. His disciples...
I have gathered these remnants of his teachings, wishing to circulate them in the world;

moreover, I sought out the surplus words of Xuedou because, from the time of the Buddhas and Patriarchs down to the present, no one has been able to withstand the piercing sting of his sharp wit. Those who read this in the future should likewise examine carefully the skillful means employed here.
The Recorded Sayings of Baxiao Yan:
When Baxiao Yan let out a single roar, it did not merely reach forty li; rather, all three thousand worlds were utterly shaken.
Fierce beasts fled and cowered, and flying birds fell from the sky. This was beyond the power of thunder to emulate, yet now that he has passed away, only his lingering resonance remains.
It still remains. Profound and resonant; it is truly impossible to conceal. Those who hear sounds with their eyes should discern this for themselves.
In the *Recorded Sayings of Shaolin*, there is one phrase that does not appear within the six assemblies of discourse. If anyone can identify it, I ask that you then burn this [record].
Record. Should it be otherwise, then from the very beginning of the text to the end of the scroll, every inch of paper and every volume will be nothing but black beans.
It does not matter; you must bite into them from the start. Who knows if, by chance, you might happen to bite upon something?
In the *Record of the Sayings of Bashikan*,
my nephew Ruiyan presented me with a volume of his elder brother Bashikan’s teachings and requested a preface.
Although I am indeed well-acquainted with my elder brother Bashikan, if Kāśyapa’s samādhi was unknown to Ānanda, then my elder brother Bashikan’s...
How could those who are ignorant of it possibly know it? If later generations wish to understand this samādhi, they cannot do so without this record;
yet they must not seek it within this record alone. If one were to truly understand it, there would be crocodiles in Chaoyang.
Regarding the Recorded Sayings of Bashittan:
My late father’s livelihood was completely ruined by my elder brother, Shittan, until nothing remained. Now, observing the aforementioned confession, it is all entirely true.
At the most grievous point, I involuntarily bit off my thumb.
Regarding the *Recorded Sayings of Da Xie*:
"He takes up the head of dead firewood and rests for a while where there is no smoke or flame. Old Master Songyuan excelled in this principle of Yangqi;

he breathed upon it and brought it forth, so that it spread widely throughout the world. Wherever he went, eminent disciples gathered like a forest of dragons and elephants. Among those who grasped its essential point was my elder brother, Da Xie.

Listen! Now, when one examines his record, although it does not possess the brilliance of a single firefly, its chilling glare is even more oppressive than the cruelty of a wildfire consuming the plains.
Those who read it should retreat seven paces.
When Dahuì retired from his duties and returned to his quarters, the head administrators came out to welcome him with a formal notice.

This is the notice issued at the time of Dahuì’s retirement. Since it says both "to reduce worldly entanglements" (*shěng yuán*) and "to cultivate stillness" (*shěng jìng*), one observes that in writing this, he was by no means truly aware [of the nature of his own mind].
While I was begging for alms in the Jiangxi countryside, the gentleman Chún held this up and sought my commentary; thus, I hastened to respond.
I wrote this while walking; it should be examined together with the *Dahui* (Great Wisdom).

Regarding the colophon to the *Pō'ān Fǎyǔ* (The Dharma Words of Old Man Pō'ān), I was standing right by his side on the day he wrote these dharma words. At that time, I involuntarily felt a surge of revulsion.
He spat it out and departed. Several decades have passed since then; how could one expect there to be anyone who would treasure it?
This is something I do not understand. The writings of Chue are utterly foolish;
his words to Shitian are unreliable from beginning to end. What Chue transcribed is garbled word for word. Nevertheless, as for the matters mentioned above...
I have no concern for my younger brother, as it would be difficult to settle the matter later on. I write this as a record. Words from Wuan (Meng Shaobao).
These words of Wuan are plain and lack literary polish;
the reader may feel like eating a soup made of wooden shavings. Nevertheless, those who possess eyes will find them upon their tongues.
It possesses its own true flavor.

This book, "Yang Xueyuan’s Discourse on Studying the Dao," is like a single milestone every five li and a double marker every ten li; those who wish to travel the path of the worthy shall not fail to obtain it.
Not viewing them as identical. Master Yang feared that they might falter midway or grow weary; therefore, he sought surplus words for the end to hasten their progress.
Although I have composed this with some effort, I fear it may instead result in clumsiness and stumbling.
Preface to *Kuchan* (Withered Chan):
In the present age, teachers and monks often suffer from a "withered" Chan, the ailment lying in the fact that they have not reached the point of total exhaustion.

This condition does not merely permeate their physical forms or manifest in their four limbs; it extends even to the eighty-four thousand pores of their skin, all of which are constantly buzzing and from which [the disease] flows out at every movement.
None can stop it. One seeks that which is free from branches and leaves, where the breath has ceased—like picking out the moon from among the stars.

The Master Cheng was deeply versed in this principle, and thus he styled himself "Dried-up Chan" (Kuchan); yet this too is merely driving a stake into empty space. Furthermore, I wish to silence Unzhu’s loquacity;
for in my ordinary life I have never engaged in such tangled entanglements with others, much less allow them within the domain of Dried-up Chan.

"Is this not a tangle? Cheng suddenly exclaimed, "There is already no small amount of tangle here. He simply laughed and wrote [this] to send to him, appending it to the end of the scroll of verses on the icchantika.
The Master Xingshang uses the term *icchantika* as his title; the general purport of this has already been seen in the work by Bai Tingyouyu.
As you seek words for your sleeve-axes (scrolls), I therefore said to him: "I, an old man, have a single phrase; I shall not decline to bring it forth."
"I simply do not know whether you, Venerable Sir, believe or do not believe. If you believe, why are you an icchantika?
If you do not believe, what benefit is there in writing this for an icchantika? When the Icchantika heard this, he looked up at the sky, shook his arm, and departed while singing a long song:
"A single bowl of rice, its fragrance pervades everywhere; Lying upon a continuous bed within a hall of seven bays. A single phrase—though the years have already passed."
"Whether one believes or not, there are those who do. Thereupon, he took up his brush and called out to them; smiling, he wrote this.
A scroll of landscapes by the attendant Bishi (with the colophons of Pō-ān, Shítian, and Chījué preceding).
Attendant Bishi showed me a small scroll of landscapes. Although the scroll is small, it contains inexhaustible meaning. It is boundless...
The meaning of "exhaustion" (jìn) cannot be described; yet that which cannot be described has already been described for me by my father and elder brothers.
What more need be said by Jingshan?
Postscript following the scroll of Yong’an.
Where function does not reach, it is used with blazing intensity. At the time of such blazing use, there is ultimately nothing that can be used.

It is like a person at night feeling for a pillow behind their back with their hands; when they use the pillow, do they still find it sweet? This was written by Jingshan at the end of the third year after [the death of] Ji'an.
In the autumn of the fifth year of the Chunyou era, I was about to lead my forces on an expedition to the south of the mountain; I appointed Bayu as my vanguard.

The youths from the four directions each devised extraordinary strategies to assist his advance. Observing their intent and assessing their momentum, it is certain that they will achieve the effect of inevitable victory and capture.
When he later returns with a triumphant banner, I shall carve a slice of the vast void as a reward.
There is something he does not begrudge. He inscribed this "Diagram of Herding an Ox":
Whose ox? Whose calf? East of the stream, west of the stream—water sweet, grass abundant. Truly fitting for the springtime at the end of the night.
Tilling the soil. It must be difficult to conceal this scroll within one’s sleeves.
As for the monk’s depiction of grasshoppers and insects:
it resembles them, yet it is not truly so. If one were a sharp-witted patch-robed monk, one would not act like such a mere insect.

I reverently present this offering of incense and tea to announce my devotion at the stupa of the late Chan Master Wuzhun Yuanzhao Fojian Fan of Mount Jing. The Master rose from Jiange;
his staff flew into Wu. Once his enlightened nature was perfected, his reputation spread far and wide. For eighteen years, he served the Dharma.

Wielding the fly-whisk at Shuangjing, you again manifested pavilions and towers; in the space of a single snap of the fingers, you demonstrated the supramundane Dharma. This is not something I can fathom.
Speaking merely from a worldly perspective, who could equal you? Why do you not live out a full hundred years to continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom, so that those monastic groves may...

Knowing that what was grasped was correct, I have written this brief letter to bid you farewell. Is the fruit of stillness truly blissful? I send forth this single incense offering; sighing and lamenting before the wind, may you still partake.
